vignette:
Kwame was seventy-eight, a retired librarian who still worked part-time at the university archive, when the memories first began to press in without warning. He had been back in his hometown for his younger sister's funeral when a bomb tore through the central market on a Saturday afternoon. The blast itself was a white flash and a deafening pressure, but what stayed with him was what came after: bodies scattered among overturned stalls, and then the looting. People he had known for years-neighbors, shopkeepers-began grabbing goods from shattered stalls while others lay bleeding. He saw a man in a bloodstained shirt calmly stuffing cassettes into a bag. That image, the casual moral unraveling, lodged deeper than the smoke and sirens. For months afterward, the memory was a clear, detailed film that played over and over, triggered by the most ordinary things: the smell of grilled meat, the sound of a crowd, or simply the turn of a calendar page.

The anniversary arrived six months later, and Kwame found himself unable to go to work. He stayed home, but the television news showed a commemorative ceremony, and he felt the full memory flood back without warning-the heat, the dust, the man with the cassettes. After that, he began to avoid crowds altogether. Shopping centres, public events, even the busy corridor between the archive and the main library became impossible. He would take long, circuitous routes or leave early. But those very routes became their own kind of trigger-each detour forced him to acknowledge what he was fleeing, and soon the sight of an alternative path or a closed shop on his new route was enough to bring the market flooding back. He also noticed that certain conversation topics-politics, faith, even discussions about community duty-made his stomach clench, because they reminded him of the betrayal he had witnessed. His wife, Adwoa, tried to draw him into family gatherings, but Kwame had come to believe that allowing himself any happiness was dangerous, as if hope would make him vulnerable to another catastrophe. He started turning down invitations to positive events-birthday parties, holiday dinners-because those situations felt like a trap. In the quiet of his home library, he would drift off into a world of his own, a fantasy where the market was peaceful and no one misbehaved. But even there, the memory sometimes surfaced, triggered by his own escape.

Over the weeks and months, a cruel cycle tightened. A trigger-the anniversary, a neighbor's loud argument, a news report about misbehavior somewhere in the world-would send Kwame into avoidance. He would cancel plans, leave a room, or sink into his fantasy world. That avoidance, in turn, made the memory stronger: the more he tried to shut it out, the more vividly the film played in his mind, and the more easily small cues brought it back. He became hypervigilant to signs of moral violation, seeing potential betrayals in everyday discourtesy-a driver honking too long, a teenager talking loudly on a bus. Each perceived misbehavior reaffirmed his dread, and he withdrew further, spending entire days in the archive's back room, alone with old catalogues, letting his mind wander to a place where none of it had happened.

The fantasy escape became his only relief, but it also fed the memory. When he snapped back to reality, the contrast was jarring, and the traumatic scene would intrude again, triggered by the very act of escaping. He stopped going to the weekly library staff meetings because someone once mentioned a protest abroad. That avoidance reinforced his belief that the world was dangerous and that joy was a prelude to disaster. His wife noticed him slipping away into long silences, and their conversations grew strained. At work, his supervisor expressed concern about his missed shifts and withdrawn manner.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a small, ordinary moment. He saw a child drop a coin in the library and another child pick it up and return it. Instead of feeling reassured, he felt a wave of panic: the gesture was so decent that it felt unreal, a setup. He knew then that his own mind had turned against trust itself. He came to the clinic because he was afraid he would never feel safe around people again, and because he missed the person he used to be-the librarian who loved the quiet hum of a busy reading room, who believed in the goodness of small acts. Now he was not sure that person still existed.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that the patient's maladaptive strategies (avoidance, fantasy escape) lead to increased triggers (triggering stimuli). Instead, triggers lead to avoidance, and avoidance strengthens memory, but the strategies do not directly cause the emergence of new triggers.
